A párharc első mérkőzését egy öngóllal a lettek nyerték, vagyis a győriek nem várták lehetetlen helyzetből a visszavágót, amelyre felépült sérüléséből Željko Gavrić, és rögtön be is került a kezdőcsapatba. Hiányzott viszont Csinger Márk és Tóth Rajmund, akik vélhetően még a nyári átigazolási időszakban távoznak a magyar bajnoktól, illetve a nyári világbajnokságon is pályára lépett algériai Nadir Benbuali továbbra is sérült. Hazai gólszerzési lehetőséggel kezdődött a találkozó, de Gavrić fejese után Baba Musah mentett a gólvonalról, aztán a játékrész felénél az ellenfél is csaknem betalált, Miljan Krpić azonban fejjel útját állta a kapuba tartó labdának. Fordulás után is a vendégek irányítottak, húsz perc alatt hét kapura lövésükből Petrás három védéssel őrizte csapata előnyét, négyszer pedig a kapu fölött vagy mellett hagyta el a labda a játékteret. Beszorult a Győr, játékosai gyakran pánikszerűen csak felszabadítottak, de a Riga máris újra a tizenhatos előterében volt. The Czech government has scrapped the programme, and funding has dropped by 70% 12. 8. 2026 / Petr Waniek Horváth Photo: the current controversial Czech PM, the oligarch Andrej Babiš For years, the New Green Savings programme was one of the Czech government’s most successful initiatives. It helped people lower their utility bills, increased the value of their homes, and had clear environmental benefits. Thanks to the subsidy, a typical family living in an older home could afford insulation that they would otherwise have put off for years—the subsidy covered roughly 30 to 50% of the costs, heating bills dropped by a third, and the home’s value rose by more than 10%. The program worked until this Czech government overhauled it beyond recognition. The Ministry of the Environment is now controlled by the [crazy] "Motorists for Themselves" party: it was first led by Petr Macinka, a longtime associate of [former Czech extreme right wing PM] Václav Klaus, and then by Igor Červený. The management style hasn’t changed, but unqualified people are replacing experts—including, for example, a warehouse worker and an 18-year-old influencer. The result is immediately apparent: interest in the program has plummeted to less than a third of its original level. How the program worked before “New Green Savings” was based on a simple principle: the state provided grants to people for energy-saving home renovations. These were not loans, but non-repayable grants that covered part of the costs of insulation, window replacement, solar panels, or a heat pump. A family with an old house and high utility bills could afford to insulate the facade thanks to the subsidy. Their bills dropped by tens of percent, and the value of their home increased. Homeowners with coal-fired boilers could switch to a heat pump, and the subsidy covered a large portion of the investment; operating costs fell, and local emissions disappeared. The program was funded by emissions allowances. Money collected from polluters was returned to people in the form of energy savings. Logical, fair, and effective. As recently as 2025, over 1,058 applications were being submitted each week—more than 54,000 projects annually, with a total requested subsidy of 27.5 billion crowns. What the Current Babiš Government Did The government halted the program, overhauled it, and introduced a system that discouraged people. It eliminated direct subsidies for most households and replaced them with interest-free loans. But a loan is not a subsidy. It’s a debt that households must repay. In times of economic uncertainty, people do not want to go into debt—and certainly not for an investment that will take years to pay off. On top of that, new administrative hurdles have been added: the renovation passport, mandatory energy performance certificates (PENB), unclear methodologies, and unclear parameters for banking products. The result is chaos in which neither applicants nor banks can find their way. And the fundamental problem is funding. Allocations from emission allowances have dropped to zero. While the implementation plan anticipated that the New Green Savings programme would receive 25% of revenue from allowances (approximately 3.7 billion CZK), the 2026 budget proposal allocated 0 CZK to the program—without explanation, without analysis, and without compensation. Furthermore, the program was suspended for nearly eight months—from November 2025 to the end of June 2026. When it reopened, only 1,759 applications were received in six weeks—roughly 28% of the original pace. Numbers That Speak for Themselves Previously, 1,058 applications were received per week. Now, the number is around 300—a 72% decline. Of the 1,759 applications, the largest share was for New Green Savings Light programme (777 applications), but this does not represent the majority. The program’s pace has simply dropped to one-third of what it was. Why These Grants Are Important The Czech Republic has one of the oldest housing stocks in the EU; the average age of buildings is around 50 years. Insulation, window replacement, and heating system modernization—all of these significantly reduce energy consumption and, consequently, household bills. Renovations also increase property value. According to available sources, this increase is 15–25% for comprehensive renovations and “more than 20%” for the insulation of apartment buildings. Subsidies are therefore not a “gift,” but an investment in citizens’ assets. And that is precisely why it is absurd that the government cut off funding for the program from emissions allowance revenues. These were supposed to be its main source of funding. Instead, the funds vanished into the budget, and people were told to take out loans. Impact on Citizens Higher energy bills, rising energy poverty, stalled projects, deteriorating technical condition of buildings, and a decline in property values. Renovations are not an “environmental fad,” but an investment that has a direct impact on living standards. When the state dismantles this mechanism, it is not just acting against the environment. It is acting against the people. The New Green Savings Program was one of the few tools that had a real impact on households’ lives. The current government has transformed it into a dysfunctional system that discourages people rather than motivating them. A 70 percent drop in applications is not a “success,” but proof of failure. And it’s a testament to a government that relies on ideology and loyalty rather than expertise. Objednat předplatné Všechno, vůči čemu jsou Britské listy opakem Primárním obsahem současných novin je komercionalizované zpravodajství zpracované tak, aby zaujalo široké publikum, aby je pobavilo, aby bylo efektivní z hlediska nákladů a aby bylo možno prodat pozornost publika zadavatelům reklamy. Výsledkem je, že jsou přehlíženy příběhy, které by mohly pohoršit, a přednost dostávají příběhy, které jsou přijatelné a zábavné pro větší počet čtenářů. Příběhy, jejichž zpracování je nákladné, jsou zlehčovány nebo opomíjeny, nevšímavě jsou přecházeny také ty příběhy, které jsou finančně riskantní. To vše vede k homogenizaci obsahu novin, k referování o bezpečných otázkách a omezení škály názorů a vyjadřovaných myšlenek. R.G. Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn A famous Romanian hacker was caught in traffic in Sinaia, Prahova County, over the weekend despite the fact that his car was equipped with an ingenious system for changing license plates. The 42-year-old man was pulled over following an alert generated by the automatic license plate recognition system installed on a police vehicle. At first, he allegedly presented fake identity documents, apparently issued by Italy, while the license plates appeared to belong to the diplomatic corps, according to Euronews Romania . During checks, police reportedly found that the car was equipped with two sets of license plates, both the fake ones observed in traffic and some real ones, plus a rotating system that allowed them to be changed quickly. In addition, the individual had a suspended driving license. He was detained, and investigations showed that he was a famous hacker. The man had run a service that allowed cybercriminals to distribute dangerous viruses, which infected more than one million computers around the world, including those belonging to NASA. The hackers stole passwords and personal data from several people in different countries, accessed their bank accounts and transferred their money. After being pursued for many years and eventually arrested in Colombia, the Romanian was extradited to the US and sentenced in 2023 to three years in prison. The US authorities confiscated USD 3.5 million from him. The man had served the sentence handed down by US judges in Romania, so he was no longer wanted by the authorities, but he preferred to drive around with two sets of license plates. “Police officers from the Sinaia Resort Police Station ordered the 24-hour detention of a 42-year-old man from the municipality of Bucharest, who is being investigated for the offenses of driving a vehicle on public roads by a person whose right to drive has been suspended, identity fraud, and putting into circulation or driving on public roads a vehicle with a false registration number,” said Alexandru Niță, spokesperson for the Prahova County Police Inspectorate. A judge, however, changed the measure to 30-day house arrest. radu@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Vlad Ispas|Dreamstime.com ) Read next 14 June 2023 Justice Romanian hacker sentenced to jail in the United States Normal Justice Famous hacker caught with false plates in Romania’s mountain resort of Sinaia 18 August 2026 Radu Dumitrescu Like this article? Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian Higher education Higher education regulator apologises for imposing £585,000 fine on university Office for Students made decision to punish University of Sussex with fine last year after claiming it breached free speech regulations Richard Adams Education editor Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.01 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 15.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google England’s higher education regulator has apologised for a string of mistakes in its decision to punish the University of Sussex with a record fine that was later overturned by the high court. The Office for Students (OfS) tried to impose a £585,000 fine against Sussex last year after claiming the university breached free speech regulations involving its former professor Kathleen Stock. It was forced to back down in April after a judicial review initiated by Sussex found the OfS “had closed its mind” and acted with bias. In a statement, the regulator said: “The OfS made mistakes in the Sussex case, which we regret. The actions we are announcing today show our continuing commitment to learning the lessons from this case with humility and honesty.” University of Sussex overturns £585,000 fine as high court rejects free speech breach claim Read more Among the changes promised by the OfS in a “lessons learned” report were “ensuring respectful relationships with higher education providers” and in the future using “alternative forms of intervention where possible to effect change” before taking enforcement action such as fines. Prof Sasha Roseneil, Sussex’s vice-chancellor, said she welcomed the OfS’s acknowledgement of its mistakes but was concerned that its plans for reform “fell short” in a number of areas. Roseneil said: “[The report] reveals deep cultural problems within the OfS in relation to freedom of expression and internal challenge, and it is heartening to see the new leadership setting different expectations for the organisation, expectations that are more appropriate for a public institution, trusted to regulate one of the most important sectors in a democratic society. “However, the report does not fully reflect the breadth or the seriousness of the high court’s findings or all the lessons that could be learned from the case. It is also disappointing that the review missed the opportunity to engage with the University of Sussex when their lack of engagement was roundly criticised by the high court.” The high court’s findings were backed up by an internal review by KPMG commissioned by the OfS, published in summary on Thursday. KPMG’s findings criticised the regulator for being adversarial, allowing gaps in its written records, and lacking clear accountability. “It appears that insufficient emphasis was placed on maintaining constructive engagement and dialogue with higher education providers, which contributed to relationships becoming increasingly adversarial,” according to the review’s summary. KPMG also criticised the OfS’s leadership at the time for becoming blinkered: “The investigation team was made up of particularly senior staff, reflecting the case’s novelty, complexity and profile. However, the concentration of decision making and delivery responsibilities within a relatively small group reduced the opportunity for independent challenge and fresh perspectives.” The OfS’s chair, Edward Peck, and chief executives Ruth Hannant and Polly Payne, thanked the University of Sussex’s leadership “for the frank discussions and insightful commentary leading to this point”. Hannant and Payne took over as the OfS’s chief executives in June and had no prior involvement with the decision to fine Sussex. The OfS investigation began after Stock’s resignation from Sussex in 2021, following campus protests for her views on transgender rights and gender identity. https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-begins-hun.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LfmS In his election campaign, Peter Magyar promised to recover government funds that were stolen or diverted by the Orban administration Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP Advertisement Asset recovery — it sounds bureaucratic but behind this phrase is one of the most important campaign promises made by Hungary's new government. Hungary's new prime minister, Peter Magyar, and his Tisza party want to retrieve funds and assets that went — in some dubious ways — to the family of ousted Hungarian leader Viktor Orban or his allies, various oligarchs, or frontmen. The new government wants those funds back for state use, and it also plans to hold the beneficiaries accountable under law. Billions of euros were stolen or diverted and, if social media is to be believed, many Hungarians want to see the individuals responsible behind bars . Magyar has talked of a sum of around €60 billion ($70 billion), though other estimates suggest the real amount could be three times that much. Orban, allies lived lives of luxury Observers say the success or failure of the asset recovery will almost certainly influence the future of Magyar and the Tisza party. The huge sums of money are linked to images of decadent luxury under Orban. The former Hungarian prime minister's family, party members, and friendly oligarchs lived on luxury estates, flew in luxury jets, vacationed on luxury yachts, and repeatedly won billions worth of public contracts. Orban-affiliated entrepreneurs , artists, academics, and journalists were also generously supported with public funds for years. Often their main qualification was loyalty to the former prime minister. Former Prime Minister Viktor Orban has alleged that his successor has 'dismantled the rule of law' since coming to power Image: Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto/picture alliance Those lifestyles contrasted with the lives led by Hungarians in poverty, the image of neglected public infrastructure, poor conditions in schools and hospitals, and the exodus of many young Hungarians from the country, as well as a huge deficit in the state budget, some 7.5% of Hungary's national income. These contrasts explain why there is such a popular desire for justice. It's been almost four months since the new Magyar government took office and anti-corruption actions have officially started. At the end of July, the new government established the National Asset Recovery Authority, or NVVH — a sort of "super institution" with very broad powers and independence. Hungary hasn't had an authority like this in its modern history. The way state assets were privatized in the 1990s after communist rule was problematic, as it often was elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. When Orban first came to power in 2010, there was a half-hearted attempt to address the corruption of the previous government under Ferenc Gyurcsany, but it came to nothing. Hungary new PM lifts lid on Orban-era government luxury To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video This time, things are meant to be different. The NVVH will investigate where public funds flowed and how assets like real estate were used. Although no specific date has been set, the investigations will primarily focus on the Orban government's time in power, so dating back to 2010. The authority is also meant to make sure this cannot happen again, and will look into how public funds and assets are to be used in future. The NVVH has both policing and prosecutorial powers, so it can investigate cases and bring charges. The authority is accountable to Hungary's parliament. Controversy around new anti-corruption body But the creation of the NVVH has not been without controversy . Late last week, parliament appointed Anna Unger, 46, a political scientist at Eotvos Lorand University in Budapest, to head the new anti-corruption and asset recovery body. Unger is an expert on political systems, democratic institutions, and party financing and was chosen out of almost 100 other applicants in a process with several stages. Some were surprised at Unger's appointment, as she wasn't really a public figure. Her research has included political corruption but she's not a recognized expert on the topic, nor is she a lawyer. Observers had expected a lawyer or an anti-corruption expert to get the job, somebody like Miklos Ligeti, head of legal affairs at Transparency International Hungary since 2012. Anna Unger was named head of the new accountability organization in late August Image: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP Ligeti also applied for the job but is reportedly being considered for a position as a deputy director. Unger will have four deputies with different duties and responsibilities. Katalin Tasnady, a well-known prosecutor with around two decades of criminal law experience, was made the NVVH's deputy chief of investigations. Government representatives said Unger had presented a comprehensive political vision for the agency's work. During her parliamentary hearing, she said that under Orban, Hungary saw more than just what one might call classic corruption. An almost feudal system had prevailed, she argued. That was why in addition to restitution and asset recovery, the system had to be thoroughly investigated and exposed so that it would never happen again, Unger said. No justice in next 6 years? Unger caused the biggest upset when she said it would be folly to expect legally binding verdicts in any major corruption cases during the NVVH's first six-year term. Robert Puzser, a popular commentator and personality on social media, called Unger's statement "devastating." Voters had given Magyar "unprecedented power to hold the country's plunderers to account," he said on Facebook, and if Hungarians had to wait more than six years, it could cause the collapse of this new government. The new prime minister himself reacted angrily to critics who said the NVVH should have had a lawyer at its head. "Nobody promised people they could vote for the leader of the NVVH as if it was a [reality TV] casting show," he wrote on Facebook. Plenty of experts thought Unger was absolutely suitable for the job. In a podcast on the 24.hu media outlet, political science Gabor Torok surmised that the way that the NVVH had been established indicated that it would be a "strong political institution" that aimed to come to terms with the recent past. Torok said the public expects the Tisza party to thoroughly reckon with the old system, and the new government will only be able to maintain the public's trust if it doesn't look like the "culprits of the previous order" are getting away with their past crimes, he said. https://www.politico.eu/article/european.text: European Investment Bank President Nadia Calviño is heading to Ottawa on Sunday to lay the groundwork for Europe-Canada cooperation on critical raw materials, an official from her office said. Calviño will be meeting with government officials including Canada’s minister for energy and natural resources, Tim Hodgson, in Ottawa. The aim of her visit is for the European Investment Bank, the long-term lending arm of the European Union, to establish a presence in Canada and begin operations “as soon as the administrative paperwork is done, with a focus on [critical raw materials],” the official said. They were granted anonymity to speak about the internal strategy. Advertisement Advertisement Coming after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed admitting Canada as an associate member of the EU, Calviño’s trip is significant given that the EIB typically only operates in developing countries or members of the European Union or European Economic Area. Ahead of this year’s G7 summit, Canada extended a behind-the-scenes offer to alliance members for “priority access” to its critical minerals stockpile, according to a letter seen by POLITICO from Hodgson. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney named boosting critical raw materials as one of the areas in which he wants to boost collaboration between Ottawa and Brussels in a speech to the European Parliament on Thursday. “Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities, including critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and computers, energy security, space and payments,” he said. Carney told an investment summit in Toronto on Tuesday that EU and Canadian leaders would get down to serious business at an end-October summit that he will host in Montreal. “The real deepening and discussions will be launched with our summit,” Carney said in Toronto. “And then go for it from there.” Mike Blanchfield contributed reporting from Ottawa.
